planting.note: Sow surface-sown seed indoors in a lean, gritty, fast-draining mix at warm temperature, or set out nursery plants after frost into lean, sandy, alkaline soil in full sun; kanna is a low, sprawling succulent from the semi-arid Karoo and needs excellent drainage above all else.

directions: Sceletium tortuosum is a mat-forming, jointed-stemmed succulent of the fig-marigold family, native to the dry Karoo and Namaqualand regions of South Africa, where the fermented leaf and stem material (traditionally called kougoed, or chew-stuff) has long been chewed, smoked, or brewed as a mood-lifting and appetite-suppressing traditional remedy. Small, star-shaped, pale yellow to white flowers open in sunny weather over succulent, fleshy, sometimes purple-tinged leaves. Grow it exactly as you would a hardy mesemb or ice plant: bone-dry, mineral soil, full sun, and minimal winter water, since rot rather than cold is the main threat in cultivation. Established plants tolerate long dry spells and light frost once mature. Container culture with a cactus-style mix is the most reliable approach outside its native climate.
sources: PROTA - Plant Resources of Tropical Africa

planting.note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container-grown stock in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun to light shade; bush tea establishes slowly and benefits from grassland-edge conditions with good air movement.

directions: Athrixia phylicoides is a wiry, heath-like shrub of South African grassland margins and forest fringes, long harvested by Zulu and other southern African communities for its narrow, resinous, silver-backed leaves, which are dried and steeped into a mild, reddish, slightly astringent herbal tea traditionally valued for soothing coughs and settling digestion. Clusters of small, daisy-like, mauve-pink flowers with yellow centers appear from late summer into autumn, giving the plant ornamental interest beyond its use as a tea herb. It responds well to light, regular tipping to keep growth dense and to encourage the fine new leaf growth preferred for harvest. Give it open, airy placement rather than dense shade, since crowding encourages dieback in humid climates.
sources: PROTA - Plant Resources of Tropical Africa
Agricultural Research Council of South Africa

planting.note: Nick or hot-water scarify seed before sowing into lean, acidic, very well-drained fynbos-type soil in full sun; honeybush is slow to establish and is usually grown from nursery-raised seedlings rather than direct field sowing outside its native range.

directions: Cyclopia subternata is a wiry, yellow-flowered legume shrub of the Cape fynbos, one of several Cyclopia species harvested for honeybush tea, a naturally sweet, caffeine-free herbal infusion made by fermenting the cut, needle-like leaves and stems until they darken and develop the tea's characteristic honey-like aroma. Bright yellow, sweetly scented, pea-like flowers appear in spring and give the plant its common name as much as the finished tea does. As with rooibos and other fynbos legumes, deep, nutrient-poor, acidic sandy soil and excellent drainage are essential; rich garden soil or wet feet quickly kill it. Established plants are cut back periodically to encourage the fine new growth used for tea production. Best suited to a dedicated fynbos or Mediterranean-climate herb bed rather than a conventional border.
sources: Agricultural Research Council of South Africa
PROTA - Plant Resources of Tropical Africa

planting.note: Scarify hard seed coat and soak overnight before sowing into lean, well-drained soil in full sun; cancer bush germinates readily once scarified and grows quickly into a flowering shrub in its first season.

directions: Lessertia frutescens (long known as Sutherlandia frutescens) is a fast-growing, silver-grey-leaved legume shrub from the dry interior of South Africa, prized in Khoisan and Cape traditional medicine as a general tonic and immune-supporting herb; the dried leaf is still sold today as a popular southern African herbal supplement. Showy, brilliant orange-red, pea-shaped flowers appear over a long season and are followed by distinctive, inflated, papery, balloon-like seed pods that give the plant strong ornamental appeal beyond its medicinal use. It is drought-tolerant once established and thrives in the same lean, sharply drained conditions favored by most Cape fynbos and Karoo herbs. Prune lightly after flowering to keep growth compact, and expect a relatively short-lived shrub of three to five years that is easily renewed from fresh seed.
sources: PROTA - Plant Resources of Tropical Africa

planting.note: Surface-sow fine seed into lean, well-drained soil in full sun and keep evenly moist until germination; impepho self-sows readily once established and needs little further care.

directions: Helichrysum odoratissimum is a strongly aromatic, woolly-grey-leaved perennial of South African grasslands, widely known as impepho and burned as dried bundled foliage in Zulu, Xhosa, and other southern African traditions to honor ancestors and cleanse a space, one of the most culturally significant smudging herbs of the region, comparable in role to white sage or sweetgrass elsewhere. The felted, silver-green leaves release a warm, honey-curry-like scent when brushed or dried, and clusters of small, papery, everlasting, golden-yellow flowers appear in summer and hold their color well after drying, making the plant useful for dried arrangements as well as ceremonial bundles. It thrives in poor, gritty soil and full sun, tolerating drought far better than excess moisture, and benefits from an annual cutback to keep growth dense and prevent legginess.
sources: PROTA - Plant Resources of Tropical Africa
